title: Lady Poverty
hook: Francis spoke of poverty as a bride: freedom from owning

segments.voice: Yesterday, heaven on earth: a room fuller than it looks. Your line was heaven is near. Where did you pause and act as if the room were full? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

A young man stands before the bishop in Assisi, a hill town in Italy. His father, a cloth merchant, is furious: the son has been giving away money and goods that the father counts as his. So the son does something nobody there expects. He hands back the money, then takes off his very clothes and hands those back too. From now on, the early accounts have him say, he'll call only God his father. The bishop wraps his own cloak around him. The young man is Francis, and he's about to fall in love with someone unexpected. A new room in the house today: the Franciscans. Today's word: Lady Poverty.

Francis spoke about poverty the way a knight in an old love song speaks of his lady. Poverty was his bride, and he courted her. One early allegory about him even turns it into a story. Francis and his brothers climb a mountain to find Lady Poverty, and bring her down to share a meal: a little bread and cold water. When she asks to see their cloister, they lead her to a hilltop and show her the whole world. This, they say, is our cloister. Why a bride, and not a burden? Because for Francis, poverty meant freedom. Things own you back. A house wants guarding, money wants counting, a fine coat wants protecting from the rain. He heard the Gospel words where Jesus sends out his disciples, "Provide neither gold, nor silver, nor brass in your purses," and tradition says he took them at face value. He looked at Jesus himself, who said, "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Owning nothing left Francis's hands free: for lepers, for the poor, for praise. It's worth being careful here. Nothing in his story makes forced hunger holy. In the early accounts, Francis chooses to share the life of the poor and stand beside them, and gives away what comes to him. Christians take his example in different ways. Franciscan friars and sisters still take vows of poverty. Others hear it as a question to carry: how much is enough, and what do my things ask of me?

Here's the practice: give away one thing. Sit, and walk through your home in your mind: a closet, a shelf, a drawer. Find one thing you don't need that someone else could use. Not the thing you'd never miss; one with a little pull to it. Hold it in your mind and notice any tug. That pull is what Francis wanted to be free of. If you pray, you can offer it to God. Then decide where it's going, and when. The bell holds the time.
Lady Poverty. Francis's name for the life of owning nothing, loved like a bride because it set him free.
Your line: free of things. Today, give that one thing away. Actually hand it over, and notice how your hands feel afterward. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Franciscan friars and sisters take a vow of poverty and hold possessions in common; lay Franciscans and other Christians inspired by Francis practice simplicity and giving in ordinary life.

original.note: Latin: Lady Poverty, the name early Franciscan writings give her.

trapdoor: what you thought: poverty just means having nothing.
what it means: Francis's chosen bride, freedom from owning so his hands were free for others.
what a scholar hears: the Sacrum Commercium, an early allegory, tells of the brothers showing Lady Poverty the world as their cloister.

notes: The scene before the bishop of Assisi is paraphrased from the early lives (Celano, Bonaventure); details vary between accounts (e.g. whether he kept a hair shirt). Confirm.
Sacrum Commercium: the climb to find Lady Poverty, the meal of bread and water, and 'this is our cloister' (showing her the world from a hill) are paraphrased. Confirm the details and the ending.
'Francis spoke about poverty the way a knight in an old love song speaks of his lady' reflects the courtly-love imagery in the early sources; confirm fair.
Matthew 10:9 linked to Francis's conversion ('tradition says he took them at face value'); the early lives connect him with the mission discourse heard at Mass. Confirm.
'Franciscan friars and sisters still take vows of poverty' is a general statement about the order; confirm wording.

Editor pass: cut 'folds them, sets the money on top' (detail not in the early lives as cited); Francis's motive ('as an equal') now attributed to the early accounts; practice no longer tells the listener they feel a tug.
Audit: match pair cut Luke 9:58 off mid-phrase ('hath not where to lay'); restored to 'hath not where to lay his head' (45 characters).
